This He will do and accomplish for us, what is pleasing to Him, through Christ. For if He wished to be a mediator between God and us, it is fitting that the Father will accomplish what is pleasing to Himself for us through Him.

author: Oecumenius
quote:
"bear with the word of encouragement." Gladly accept the encouragement sent to you through the letters from me. Paul does not say, of counsel or exhortation, but, because of the tribulations in which they were, he speaks of encouragement, that is, of consolation, of the call to endure.
"for I have written to you briefly." Briefly, as it relates to what is to be said in the future, there are indeed many things, if everything has been said.

author: Oecumenius
quote:
"You should know that our brother Timothy has been released." Rather, they did not have a grudge against Timothy, which is why Paul writes about him. What does it mean, "released"? Either that he was in prison and was released; or that he was being released from Athens, because he was there.
"with whom I shall see you if he comes soon." Timothy was released; but if he comes to me soon, I will see you together with him, coming to you. For it was likely that he had been released, but had not yet gone to Paul.

author: Oecumenius
quote:
"Greet all your leaders." See how Paul honors them, for he addresses the leaders through them; for it was more fitting to command the leaders and to address the ones being led through them; but he wisely heals the weaker ones.
"Those from Italy greet you." Therefore, I am so filled with you that not only do I greet you myself, but I also establish such a longing towards you in others, that even from such a distance they desire you, and for this reason, they greet you.

author: Oecumenius
quote:
"Grace be with all of you." Since grace is something common, it is prayed for mutually for all, both leaders and those being led. But what is grace? It is the forgiveness of sins, the cleansing, the participation in the Spirit. How can it be with you all? If you do not insult the support of God, sinning and being negligent, if you do not live unworthily of it. For grace remains when we have good works; it departs when we do not live according to the command of the one who gives it to us. But let it be, knowing this, and all that we have received through it, not to conduct ourselves in arrogance towards such great goods bestowed upon us; but through good works glorifying Him, and showing that this grace was not given to ungrateful and thankless people, to have it unyielding in our souls, in Christ Himself, the supporter of our souls. With whom be glory to the Father, together with the Holy Spirit, now and always, and until forever and ever. Amen.
The end, with the aid of divine favor, of the Epistle to the Hebrews.
It was written from Italy by Timothy.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: In my opinion, the Son is the reflection of the total glory of God, according to Paul who said, "He reflects the glory of God," anticipating, however, a partial reflection on the rest of the rational creation from this reflection of the total glory. For I do not think that anyone except the Son can contain the whole reflection of the full glory of God.
source_title: COMMENTARY ON THE GOSPEL OF JOHN 32.353

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Now this Son was begotten of the Father's will, for he is the "image of the invisible God" and the "effulgence of God's glory and the impress of God's substance." … Let those who dare to say, "There was a time when the Son was not" understand that this is what they are saying: "Once wisdom did not exist, and word did not exist, and life did not exist." But it is not right, nor is it safe for us, in our weakness to rob God … of God's only begotten Word, who ever dwells with God, who is God's wisdom, in whom God rejoiced. For if we do this, we shall think of God as not always rejoicing.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: The apostle Paul says, that the only begotten Son is … "the brightness of his glory, and the express image of his person." Now, we find in the treatise called the Wisdom of Solomon the following description of the wisdom of God: "For she is the breath of the power of God, and the purest emanation of the glory of the Almighty." Nothing that is polluted can therefore come upon her, for she is the splendor of the eternal light, the stainless mirror of God's working and the image of his goodness. Now we say, as before, that Wisdom has her existence nowhere else but in him who is the beginning of all things, from whom also is derived everything that is wise, because he himself is the only one who is by nature a Son, and is therefore called the Only Begotten.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: In order … to more completely understand how the Savior is the figure of the person or subsistence of God, let us use an illustration. While it does not describe the subject of which we are treating either fully or appropriately, it may nevertheless be employed for this purpose only: to show that when the Son of God, who was in the form of God, emptied himself, his object was to display to us by this very emptying the fullness of his deity. For instance, suppose that there were a statue of so enormous a size as to fill the whole world, and because of this could be seen by no one. If another statue were formed altogether resembling it in the shape of the limbs, and in the outline of features, and in form and material, but without the same immensity of size, then those who were unable to behold the one of enormous proportions, should, on seeing the latter, acknowledge that they had seen the former, because it preserved all the features of its limbs and appearance, and even the very form and material, so closely as to be altogether undistinguishable from it.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Let us see, then, what the devil speaks to the Lord from the Scriptures: "For it is written, that he has commanded his angels concerning you, and in their hands they will lift you up, lest perhaps you dash your foot against a stone." See how, even in the testimonies themselves, he is shifty. For he wishes to diminish the glory of the Savior, as though he needed the help of the angels, being about to dash his foot unless he were lifted up by their hands. He takes up a testimony and interprets of Christ that which was written not of Christ, but of the saints generally. For freely and with all confidence I contradict the devil, that this cannot be understood of the person of Christ. For he does not need the help of the angels, who is greater than the angels and has obtained by inheritance a name better than they. To none of the angels did God ever say: "You are my Son, this day have I begotten you." To none of them did he speak as to a son, "he who makes his angels spirits, and his ministers a burning fire," but to his own proper Son, of whom he speaks innumerable things in the prophets. He does not need, I say, the help of the angels, the Son of God. Nay rather, learn, O devil, that, unless Jesus should help the angels, they dash their own foot. And if any of the angels has seemed to dash his foot—of whom it was read a little while ago: "that we shall judge angels"—he dashes it for this reason, that he did not stretch out his hand to Jesus, so that, being grasped by him, he might not dash it. For when anyone, trusting in his own strength, does not call upon the protection of Jesus, he dashes his foot and falls.
source_title: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 31

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: On this account our heart must be kept with all carefulness both by day and night, and no place be given to the devil. But every effort must be used that the ministers of God—those spirits who were sent to minister to those who are called to be heirs of salvation—may find a place within us, and be delighted to enter into the guest-chamber of our soul. And, dwelling within us [they] may guide us by their counsel; if, so, they shall find the habitation of our heart adorned by the practice of virtue and holiness.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: That both good angels are present to men and adverse ones; that it was surely not by chance and without judgment that that angel was allotted to be the guardian of that soul, for example of Peter, and another of Paul, or another of one infant of the Church, concerning whose angels the Lord says that they "always behold the face of their Father who is in heaven." Concerning whom there is surely no room to doubt that, by the judgment of God—who clearly perceives both their worthiness and the quality of our soul—they are allotted the guardianship of each one of us by a certain mystical lot directed by the dispensation of Christ.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: The design of Judas, also, respecting the betrayal of our Lord and Saviour, did not originate in the wickedness of his mind alone. For Scripture testifies that the "devil had already put it into his heart to betray Him." And therefore Solomon rightly commanded, saying, "Keep thy heart with all diligence." And the Apostle Paul warns us: "Therefore we ought to give the more earnest heed to the things which we have heard, lest perhaps we should let them slip." And when he says, "Neither give place to the devil," he shows by that injunction that it is through certain acts, or a kind of mental slothfulness, that room is made for the devil, so that, if he once enter our heart, he will either gain possession of us, or at least will pollute the soul, if he has not obtained the entire mastery over it, by casting on us his fiery darts; and by these we are sometimes deeply wounded, and sometimes only set on fire.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote:
We understood the Christ to be the creator, but the Father is greater. He, indeed, who is such great things as "the advocate," "the expiation," "the propitiatory," because he showed compassion "on our weaknesses" in experiencing temptation "in all things" human "in our likeness, without sin," is a "great high priest" who offered himself as the sacrifice offered once for all, not for humans alone, but also for every spiritual being. For "apart from God he tasted death for all." This appears in some copies of the epistle to the Hebrews as "by the grace of God."But whether "apart from God he tasted death for all," he died not only for humans but also for the rest of the spiritual beings, or "by the grace of God he tasted death for all," he died for all apart from God, for "by the grace of God he tasted death for all." And, indeed, it would be strange to declare that he tasted death for human sins but not also for any other creature, besides man, that happened to be in sin—for instance, for the stars, since not even the stars are absolutely pure before God. As we have read in Job, "And the stars are not clean in his sight," unless this was said hyperbolically.
For this reason he is a "great high priest," since he restores all things to the kingdom of the Father, causing the things that are lacking in each of the creatures to be supplied, that they may be able to receive the Father's glory.
source_title: COMMENTARY ON THE GOSPEL OF JOHN 1.255-58

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: How is it possible for it to be said by the Apostle concerning God: "the Only One who has immortality"? Let us investigate, and we shall discover, that Christ Jesus tasted death for everyone, except for God. This is how the one God has immortality.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: It does not suffice for them to cry 'Holy!' once, nor twice, but they take up the perfect number of the Trinity, that they may manifest the multitude of the holiness of God, which is the repeated commonalty of a threefold holiness; to the holiness of the Father is joined the holiness of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. "For both He who sanctifies and those who are sanctified are all of one". He who "sanctifies" is the Savior, according to this—that as a man He receives holiness from God the Father.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: The Apostle, recalling this saying, "Behold, I and the children whom God has given me," then goes on and expounds: "Since therefore the children shared in blood and flesh, he too became near to them, being made a partaker of theirs, that through death he might destroy him who had the dominion of death, that is, the devil, and deliver those who through fear of death were, throughout their whole life, subject to the guilt of bondage." Therefore, "since the children were made partakers of blood and flesh," our Savior too "shared in blood and flesh." For it was foreign to his nature and his divinity to take up "blood and flesh"; but for our sake he took up those things which were foreign to him, that he might make us his own household, who had been made foreign through sin. And the Apostle indeed expounded it thus, saying: "Since therefore the children shared in blood and flesh, he too became near to them, being made a partaker of theirs"; but I would say that, just as "since the children shared in blood and flesh, he too became near to them, being made a partaker of theirs," so, since the "children" cannot hear the stronger discourses — for they must, as "children," hear the words of God — for this reason, having been "made present" in the "blood of the children" for the sake of those who "shared in flesh and blood," speaking "as to little ones," he speaks not divine and unutterable things, but only such things as "little ones" can grasp.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: The texts of the New Testament, which we have discussed, are things said by Himself about Himself. Isaiah, however, He said that His mouth had been set by His Father as a sharp sword, and that He was hidden under the shadow of His hand, made like to a chosen shaft and kept close in the Father's quiver, called His servant by the God of all things, and Israel, and Light of the Gentiles. The mouth of the Son of God is a sharp sword, for "The word of God is living, and active, and sharper than any two-edged sword, and piercing to the dividing of soul and spirit, of both joints and marrow, and quick to discern the thoughts and intents of the heart." And indeed He came not to bring peace on the earth, that is, to corporeal and sensible things, but a sword, and to cut through, if I may say so, the disastrous friendship of soul and body, so that the soul, committing herself to the spirit which was against the flesh, may enter into friendship with God. Hence, according to the prophetic word, He made His mouth as a sword, as a sharp sword. Can any one behold so many wounded by the divine love, like her in the Song of Songs, who complained that she was wounded: "I am wounded with love," and find the dart that wounded so many souls for the love of God, in any but Him who said, "He hath made Me as a chosen shaft."
source_title: COMMENTARY ON THE GOSPEL OF JOHN 1.229

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Jesus endured the cross, disregarding the shame, and therefore is seated at the right hand of God. And those who imitate him by disregarding the shame shall sit with him and rule in the heavens with him, who came not to bring peace upon the earth but upon the souls of his followers and to bring a sword upon the earth. Since "the Word of God is living and active, sharper than any two-edged sword, piercing to the division of soul and spirit, of joints and marrow, and discerning the thoughts and intentions of the heart," this word above all now bestows on our souls the prize of that peace which surpasses all understanding, which he left to his apostles. And it brings a sword between the earthly image and the heavenly in order that when he receives our heavenly image we may be made fully heavenly, if we are worthy not to be cut in two.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: The Apostle Paul teaches us what this sword is, when he says: "for the word of God is living and effective and more penetrating than every two-edged sword, reaching even to the joint of soul and spirit, of the members also and the marrows, and is a discerner of the thoughts and intentions of the heart". This is the "sword" by whose edge "our enemies shall fall". For it is the word of God which lays low "all enemies" and puts them "under His feet", "that the whole world may be made subject to God". Do you wish to learn still from another epistle of Paul that the sword is the word of God? Hear him, when he prepares arms for the soldiers of Christ, how he says: "and take the helmet of salvation, and the sword of the spirit, which is the word of God, through all prayer and supplication", most evidently pronouncing also through these things that by "the word of God", which is "the two-edged sword", "our enemies shall fall before us".

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: I think that the saints, as they depart from this life, will remain in some place situated on the earth that the divine scripture calls "paradise." This will be a place of instruction and, so to speak, a lecture room or school for souls, in which they may be taught about all that they had seen on earth. They may also receive some indications of what is to follow in the future, just as … in this life they had obtained certain indications of the future, seen indeed "through a glass darkly" and truly "in part," which are revealed more clearly and brightly to the saints in their proper times and places. If any are "pure in heart" and of unpolluted mind and well-trained understanding, they will make swifter progress and quickly ascend to the region of the air until they reach the kingdom of the heavens, passing through the series of those "rooms," if I may so call them, which the Greeks have termed spheres, that is, globes, but which the divine Scripture calls heavens. In each of these they will first observe all that happens there and then learn the reason why it happens; and thus they will proceed in order through each stage, following him who has "passed through the heavens, Jesus the Son of God," and who has said, "I desire that they also may be with me where I am." Further, he alludes to this diversity of places when he says, "In my Father's house are many rooms." He himself, however, is everywhere and runs through all things. And we are no longer to think of him as being confined within those narrow limits in which he once lived for our sakes, that is, in that circumscribed condition which was his when he dwelt on earth among humans in a body like ours, so that it was then possible to think of him as being enclosed in some one place.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: You will ascertain a right understanding of this Scripture and others if in Christ you are fond of learning and you rise above learning "through a mirror" and "in an enigma," desiring to rush to him who calls. And you will approach knowing "face to face," as friends of your Father and teacher in heaven. For friends learn not through enigmas but by what is seen or by wisdom stripped of sounds, speech, symbols and types, attending to the nature of things perceived and the beauty of truth. If you believe that Paul was caught up to the third heaven and was caught up in paradise and heard what cannot be expressed, which no one may utter, you will then know the unexpressed things which were revealed to Paul when he descended from the third heaven. At once you will know more and greater things, after the revealing and descent, if you take up the cross and follow after Jesus, in whom we have a great high priest who has passed through the heavens. And you yourselves will pass through the heavens if you do not fail to follow him, rising above not only the earth and the mysteries of earth, but also heaven and its mysteries. For in God there are many greater things treasured up than these visions, which no bodily nature can attain unless it first is set free from all that is corporeal. For I am persuaded that God has stored up and keeps for himself many greater things than these, which the sun and moon and company of stars and even the holy angels know of, which God made by wind and flame of fire. He has done this so that he may reveal them, when all creation is set free from slavery to the enemy and obtains the glorious freedom of the children of God.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: For we do everything in our power to see that our gathering consists of intelligent people, and we dare to bring forward in common discourse at the time of our gathering our most noble and divine beliefs when we have an intelligent audience. But we conceal and pass over the more profound truths whenever we see that the meeting consists of simple-minded folk who are in need of that teaching which is figuratively called milk.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: For in the words of the Song of Songs there is that food of which the Apostle speaks: "But solid food belongs to the perfect" … And indeed the little ones whom we have mentioned, if they should come to these passages, it may be that they will gain nothing from this Scripture, yet neither will they be greatly harmed … For, not knowing how to hear the names of love with pure and chaste ears … For this reason, therefore, I give warning and counsel to everyone who is not yet free from the troubles of flesh and blood … that he abstain wholly from the reading of this little book … For they say that among the Hebrews this too is observed: that unless a man has arrived at a perfect and mature age, he is not even permitted to hold this little book in his hands … together with those which they call deuteroseis, these four things are reserved to the last — that is, the beginning of Genesis … and the beginnings of the prophet Ezekiel … and the end, in which the building of the temple is contained; and this book of the Song of Songs.
source_title: COMMENTARY ON THE SONG OF SONGS, PROLOGUE

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: But just as the doctrine of providence is not at all weakened because of those things which are not understood by those who have once honestly accepted it, so neither is the divine character of Scripture, which extends to the whole of it, lost because our weakness cannot discover in every expression the hidden splendor of the doctrines concealed in common and unattractive style. For "we have the treasure in earthen vessels, that the exceeding greatness of the power of God may shine forth" and may not be reckoned as coming from us who are but human beings.… Therefore, since a celestial or even a supercelestial power compels us to worship the only Creator, let us leave the doctrine of the beginning of Christ, i.e., the elements, and "endeavor to go on to perfection," in order that the wisdom spoken to the perfect may be spoken also to us.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Now we ought to be aware that there are some Lazaruses even now who, after having become friends of Jesus, have become sick and died. As dead persons they have remained in the tomb and the land of the dead with the dead.… Consider the one who has fallen away from Christ and returned to the Gentiles' life after he has received knowledge of the truth. He has been enlightened and tasted the heavenly gift and become a partaker of the Holy Spirit … yet now is in hades with the shades and the dead and to be in the land of the dead or the tombs.Whenever, therefore, on behalf of such a person, Jesus comes to his tomb and, standing outside it, prays and is heard, he asks that there be power in his voice and words, and he cries out with a loud voice to summon him who was his friend to the things outside the life of the Gentiles and their tomb and cave.
source_title: COMMENTARY ON THE GOSPEL OF JOHN 28.54-56

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Knowing this, the Apostle Paul also said: "For the earth, drinking in the rain that comes often upon it and bearing herb fit for those by whom it is tilled, receives blessings from God; but that which brings forth thorns and thistles is reprobate and near to a curse, whose end is unto burning". Did the Apostle say these things about this earth? But neither does the earth receive blessings from God "when it has drunk in the showers" and produced fruit; nor, if after the rain "it has brought forth thorns and thistles", does it obtain curses from God. But our earth, that is, our heart, if it should receive "the rain that comes frequently upon it" of the doctrine of the law and should bring forth the fruit of works, receives blessings. But if it should have, not spiritual work, but "thorns and thistles", that is, the cares of the world, or the desires of pleasures and riches, it is "reprobate and near to a curse, whose end will be unto burning". Therefore each one of the hearers, when he comes together to hear, receives "the shower" of the word of God; and if indeed he has brought forth the fruit of a good work, he will obtain "blessing"; but if he has despised the word of God he has received, and has neglected what he has often heard, and has subjected himself to the care of worldly affairs and to lust, as one who has choked the word with "thorns", he will procure "a curse" instead of a blessing, and instead of the end of beatitude he will find "the end of burning".

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Let us see then whether by an illustration used by the apostle in the epistle to the Hebrews, we are able to prove that by one operation God has mercy upon one while he hardens another. It is not God's intent to harden, but while having a good purpose, hardening follows as a result of the inherent principle of wickedness in such persons, so that he is said to harden him who is hardened. … As regards the rain there is one operation, but the ground which is cultivated produces fruit, while that which is neglected and is barren produces thorns.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote:
Just as the people of old, who were called the people of God, were divided into twelve tribes plus the levitical order, and this order itself, which engaged in service of the Divine, was divided into additional priestly and levitical orders, so, I think, all the people of Christ according to "the hidden person of the heart," who bear the name "Jew inwardly" and who have been circumcised "in spirit," possess the characteristics of the tribes in a more mystical manner.…Most of us who approach the teachings of Christ, since we have much time for the activities of life and offer a few acts to God, would perhaps be those from the tribes who have a little fellowship with the priests and support the service of God in a few things. But those who devote themselves to the divine Word and truly exist by the service of God alone will properly be said to be Levites and priests in accordance with the excellence of their activities in this work.
And, perhaps, those who excel all others and who hold, as it were, the first places of their generation will be high priests according to the order of Aaron, but not according to the order of Melchizedek. If someone should object to this, thinking that we are impious when we prescribe the title of high priest for humans, since Jesus is proclaimed as great priest in many places—for we have "a great high priest who has passed through the heavens, Jesus, the Son of God"—we would have to say to him that the apostle indicated this when he said that the prophet said of Christ, "You are a priest forever after the order of Melchizedek," and not after the order of Aaron. On this basis, we too say that humans can be high priests according to the order of Aaron, but only the Christ of God according to the order of Melchizedek.
source_title: COMMENTARY ON THE GOSPEL OF JOHN 1.1, 1.10-11

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Consider also of what sort this is: that in the law the face of Moses is indeed reported as glorified, though it be covered with a veil; but his hand, put "within his bosom," is recorded as "made leprous like snow." In which there seems to me to be most fully depicted the form of the whole law; for in his face is designated the word of the law, in his hand its works. Since, therefore, "by the works of the law no one was to be justified," nor could the law bring anyone "to perfection," for that reason the hand of Moses is made "leprous" and is hidden away "in his bosom," as though destined to have no perfect work; but his face is glorified, yet is covered with a veil, because his word has the glory of knowledge, but hidden.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: For all these things, therefore, he "now stands before the face of God", "interceding for us", he stands at the altar, that he may offer propitiation for us to God; and therefore, as one about to approach that altar, he said: "that I will no longer drink of the generation of this vine, until I drink it new with you". He waits, therefore, that we may be converted, that we may imitate his example, that we may follow his footsteps, and that he may rejoice with us and "drink wine with us in the kingdom of his Father". For now, because "the Lord is merciful and compassionate", he himself with greater affection than his Apostle "weeps with them that weep and desires to rejoice with them that rejoice". And much more "does he himself mourn those who sinned before and did not do penance". For it must not be thought that Paul indeed mourns for sinners and weeps for the offending, but that my Lord Jesus refrains from weeping when he approaches the Father, when he stands at the altar and offers propitiation for us; and this is, being "one who approaches the altar", not to drink the wine of gladness, because he still suffers the bitternesses of our sins. He does not will, then, to drink wine alone "in the kingdom" of God; he waits for us; for thus he said: "until I drink it with you". It is we, therefore, who, by neglecting our life, delay his gladness.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Now if we correctly understand it, this is the statement Moses writes in the beginning of his book, when he says, "In the beginning God created the heavens and the earth." For this is the beginning of all creation: to this beginning the end and consummation of all things must return. That is, that heaven and earth may be the dwelling place and rest of the pious, so that all the saints and the meek may first obtain an inheritance in that earth, for this is the teaching of the law and the prophets and the gospel. In that earth I believe there exist, the true and living forms of worship which Moses handed down under the shadow of the law. For it is said that "they serve as a copy and shadow of the heavenly sanctuary"—that is, those who were in subjection in the law. To Moses himself it was also said, "See that you make everything according to the pattern which was shown you on the mountain." It seems to me, therefore, that on this earth the law was a kind of schoolmaster to those who by it were to be led to Christ and to be instructed and trained in order that, after the training of the law, they might more easily receive the more perfect precepts of Christ. So also that other earth, which receives into it all the saints, may first imbue and mould them by the precepts of the true and everlasting law, that they may more easily gain possession of those perfect precepts of heaven, to which nothing can be added. And in heaven there will truly be what is called the "eternal gospel" and that testament that is always new, which shall never grow old.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: But who could more properly speak to us about who God is than the Son? "For no one knows the Father except the Son." We too aspire to know how God is Spirit as the Son reveals it and to worship God in the Spirit that gives life and not in the letter that kills. We want to honor God in truth and no longer in types, shadows and examples, even as the angels do not serve God in examples and the shadow of heavenly realities but in realities that belong to the spiritual and heavenly order, having a high priest of the order of Melchizedek as leader of the saving worship for those who need both the mystical and secret contemplation.
source_title: COMMENTARY ON THE GOSPEL OF JOHN 13.146

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: The apostle says with reference to the law that they who have circumcision in the flesh "serve as the copy and shadow of heavenly things." And in another place, "is not our life on earth a shadow?" If then both the law that is on the earth is a "shadow" and all our life that is on earth is the same, and we live among nations under the "shadow of Christ," we must consider whether the truth of all these shadows will be learned in that revelation when, no longer "through a mirror and darkly," but "face to face" all the saints shall be counted worthy to behold the glory of God and the causes and truth of things. And the pledge of this truth being already received through the Holy Spirit, the apostle said, "Even if we have known Christ after the flesh, yet now henceforth we know him no more.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Since, however, "when he was raised from the dead, his disciples remembered that he had said this, and they believed the Scripture and the word which Jesus had spoken," we must admit, as far as the literal meaning is concerned, that, after the Lord was raised from the dead, the disciples understood that the things said about the temple refer to his passion and resurrection, and they recalled that the saying, "in three days I will raise it up" indicated the resurrection. It was then that "they believed both the Scripture and the word which Jesus had spoken," since there is no earlier testimony that they had believed the Scripture or this word which Jesus spoke. For faith is, strictly speaking, the acceptance with one's whole soul of the object of faith at baptism. But as for the anagogical meaning, since we previously mentioned the resurrection from the dead of the whole body of the Lord, we must know that the disciples—once they were reminded through the fulfillments of the Scripture which they had not thoroughly understood when they were in this life and once it was brought before their eyes and made manifest that it contained an example and shadow of certain heavenly things—believed what they formerly did not believe, and believed the word of Jesus as he who spoke it intended, which they had not understood before the resurrection.For how can one be said to believe the Scripture in the proper sense, when one does not perceive the meaning of the Holy Spirit in it which God wants to be believed, rather than the intent of the letter? According to this, we must say that none of those who walk according to the flesh believe in the spiritual meanings of the law, whose first principle they do not even imagine.
source_title: COMMENTARY ON THE GOSPEL OF JOHN 10.298-300

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Concerning this tabernacle the divine Scriptures make mention indeed in many places and seem to indicate certain things which human hearing could scarcely be capable of; yet above all the Apostle Paul, concerning the understanding of the tabernacle, discloses to us certain tokens of a more exalted knowledge, but, in some way — perhaps regarding the frailty of his hearers — he in a manner closes up the very things that he opens. For he says, writing to the Hebrews: "For the first tabernacle was made, in which were the candlestick and the setting-forth of the loaves, which was called the holy of holies. But after the second veil the tabernacle, which is called holy, having the golden altar of incense and the ark of the testament, and within it the two tables, and the manna and the rod of Aaron, which had put forth leaves". But to these things he added: "of which it is not now to be spoken one by one". Now that he says, "of which it is not now to be spoken", some refer to that time at which he was writing the epistle to the Hebrews; but to others it seems that, on account of the greatness of the mysteries, he denies that all the time of the present life is fit for explaining these things. Yet the Apostle does not leave us wholly sorrowful, but, as is his custom, he opens a few things out of many, so that it may indeed be closed to the negligent, but found by those who seek, and opened to those who knock. He resumes therefore again concerning the tabernacle and says: "For Jesus entered not into the holy places made by hand, the copies of the true, but into heaven itself, that he may now appear before the face of God through the veil, that is, through his own flesh". He therefore who interpreted the veil of the inner tabernacle as the flesh of Christ, and the holy places themselves as heaven or the heavens, and the Lord Christ indeed as the high priest, and says that he entered "once into the holy places, having found eternal redemption" — if from these few words anyone knows how to understand the sense of Paul, he can perceive how great a sea of understanding he has opened up to us. But those who love the letter of the law of Moses well enough, yet flee its spirit, hold the Apostle Paul under suspicion for bringing forth interpretations of this kind.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: We indeed, who are of the Church, rightly receive Moses and read his writings, understanding this about him: that he is a prophet, and that, by God's revealing to him, he wrote down in symbols and figures and allegorical forms the mysteries to come, which we teach to have been fulfilled in their own time. But whoever does not receive in him a meaning of this kind, whether he be one of the Jews or even one of our own, cannot show him to be a prophet at all; for how will he prove him a prophet, whose letters he asserts to be commonplace, aware of nothing future and containing no hidden mystery? And so, as this man who thinks in this way reads these things, the divine word rebukes him and says: "Do you suppose you understand what you read?" There is, then, the law, and all the things that are in the law, according to the Apostle's judgment, "imposed until the time of correction"; and just as those whose craft it is to make figures out of bronze and to cast statues, before they produce the true work of bronze or of silver or of gold, first form a model of clay after the likeness of the image to come — which model is indeed necessary, but only until the principal work is completed; and when that work has been finished for the sake of which the model of clay had been formed, its use is no longer sought — something of this sort understand also in those things which were either written or done "in a type" and figure of things to come in the law and the prophets. For the very craftsman and author of all things came, and transferred "the law, which had the shadow of the good things to come," to "the very image of the realities." But lest perhaps the things we say seem hard to be proved to you, examine them one by one. Formerly there was Jerusalem, that great royal city, where a most famous temple had been built to God. But after he came who was the true temple of God and said of the temple of his body, "Destroy this temple," and who began to open the mysteries of the "heavenly Jerusalem": that earthly one was destroyed, where the "heavenly" one appeared, and in that temple there did not remain "stone upon stone," from the time that the flesh of Christ became the true temple of God. Formerly there was a high priest purifying the people "with the blood of bulls and goats"; but from the time the true high priest came, who by his own blood should sanctify believers, that former high priest is nowhere, nor has any place been left to him. Formerly there was an altar, and sacrifices were celebrated; but when the true lamb came, who "offered himself as a victim to God," all those things, as set in place for a time, ceased. Does it not then seem to you that, according to the figure which we set forth above, they were as it were forms fashioned out of clay, through which the images of the truth were expressed? And so, finally, the divine dispensation took care that both the city itself and the temple and all those things should alike be overthrown; lest perhaps one still "a little one and a suckling in the faith," if he saw those things standing firm, while he gazes astonished at the rite of the sacrifices and the order of the ministrations, should be carried away by the very sight of the diverse forms. But God, providing for our weakness and willing to multiply his Church, caused all those things to be overthrown and utterly removed, so that, without any hesitation, once those had ceased, we might believe these to be true, for which the type had gone before in those.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Yet it must be observed that the priest uses one set of garments while he is in the ministry of the sacrifices, and another when he goes forth to the people. This Paul too did, most learned of high priests and most skilled of priests. He who, when he was in the assembly of the perfect, as though placed within the "holy of holies" and clothed in the robe of perfection, said: "we speak wisdom among the perfect, yet a wisdom not of this world nor of the princes of this world, who are being destroyed; but we speak the wisdom of God hidden in a mystery, which none of the princes of this age knew. For if they had known, they would never have crucified the Lord of majesty." But after these things, as though "going out to the people," he changes his robe and is clothed with another far inferior to that one. And what does he say? "I judged," he says, "that I knew nothing else among you except Jesus Christ, and him crucified." You see, therefore, this most learned priest, how, when he is within among the perfect, as it were in the "holy of holies," he uses one robe of doctrine; but when he "goes out" to those who are incapable, he changes the robe of the word and teaches lower things, and gives some "milk" to drink as "little ones," nourishes others with "vegetables" as "weak," but for others prepares "strong food" — namely for those who "according to their capacity of receiving have their senses exercised for the discernment of good or evil." Thus Paul knew how to change robes and to use some for the people, others in the ministry of holy things. But he himself, the high priest of high priests and priest of priests, our Lord and Savior, of whom the Apostle says that "he is the high priest of the good things to come" — hear how he first did these things and thus left them to his disciples to be imitated. The Gospel relates concerning him and says that: "he spoke to the crowds in parables, and without a parable he did not speak to them, but privately he resolved these things for his disciples." You see how he himself taught that the high priest ought to use certain garments when he goes forth "to the crowds," and others when he ministers to the learned and "perfect" in holy things. Whence it is to be desired by us and to be striven for, that Jesus not find us such — so unprepared and so bound up with the cares of the world — that he speak to us as with the crowds "in parables," so that "seeing we do not see and hearing we do not hear"; but rather that we may merit to be found among those to whom he says: "to you it is given to know the mysteries of the kingdom of God."

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: These are the things that the letter of the law sets forth for us, so that, gathering from them the seeds of the sacred mysteries, we may ascend as by certain steps from lowly things to lofty ones and from earthly things to heavenly ones. Ascend therefore now, O hearer, if you can, and be lifted up from earthly senses by the gaze of the mind and the keenness of the heart. Forget earthly things for a little while, and walk with the step of the mind above the clouds and above the very heaven. There seek the tabernacle of God, where as a forerunner for us Jesus entered and now stands before the face of God, interceding for us. There, I say, seek those fourfold orders and stations of the camps, there behold the Israelite ranks and the watches of the saints, and there examine those mysteries of the firstborn which we now seek here.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Paul therefore, writing to the Hebrews, namely to those who indeed read the law and had these things meditated upon and well known, but had need of understanding as to how one ought to think concerning the sacrifices, says in this manner: "for Jesus entered not into the holy place made with hands, the copies of the true things, but into heaven itself, that he might now appear before the face of God for us." And again he says of the victims: "for this he did once, by offering himself as a victim." But why do we seek testimonies concerning these things one by one? If anyone should review the whole epistle itself written to the Hebrews, and especially that passage where he compares the high priest of the law with the high priest of the promise, of whom it is written: "you are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek", he will find how this whole passage of the Apostle shows those things which are written in the law to be "copies" and "forms" of living and true things.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: If the ancient custom of the sacrifices has been made clear to you, let us see what these things also contain according to the mystical reason. You have heard of two houses, one as it were visible and open to the priests, the other as it were invisible and inaccessible: except the one high priest alone, the rest are outside. This first house I think can be understood to be this in which we now are, placed in the flesh, the church, in which the priests minister "at the altar of the whole burnt offerings", that fire being kindled of which Jesus said: "I came to send fire upon the earth, and how I wish that it be kindled". And I do not wish you to marvel that this house lies open to the priests alone. For all, whoever have been anointed with the ointment of the sacred chrism, have been made priests, as Peter too says to the whole church: "but you are a chosen race, royal, priestly, a holy nation". You are therefore a "priestly race" and therefore you approach the holy things.… In this way therefore the priesthood is carried out in the first house and the victims are offered, and from this house the high priest, clothed with sanctified garments, sets forth and enters into the interior of the veil, as we have already above set down the words of Paul saying: "not into the holy place made with hands, but into heaven itself Jesus penetrated" it says, "and appears before the face of God for us". Therefore the place of heaven and the very seat of God is designated through the figure and image of the interior house.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: But this world, which is itself called an "age," is said to be the end of many ages. Now the holy apostle teaches that in the age that was before this, Christ did not suffer, nor even in the age before that; and I do not know that I am able to enumerate the number of previous ages in which he did not suffer. I will show, however, the statements of Paul from which I have arrived at this understanding. He says, "He has appeared once for all at the end of the age to take away sin by the sacrifice of himself." He says that Christ was made a "sacrifice" once, and "at the end of the ages has appeared to take away sin." Now after this age, which is said to be made for the consummation of other ages, there will be other ages again to follow; for we have clearly learned this from Paul himself, who says, "that in the ages to come he might show the immeasurable riches of his grace in his kindness toward us." He did not say "in the age to come" or "in the two ages to come" but "in the ages to come." I think, therefore, that by his language many ages are indicated.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: In trying to reconcile two apostolic passages it has often occurred to me to raise the question of how there can be a consummation of ages at which Jesus has been manifested once for all to do away with sin if there are going to be ages following this age. The passages are these: In Hebrews, "But now at a consummation of the ages he has been manifested once for all to do away with sin through his sacrifice," but in Ephesians, "In order that he may show forth in the years following, the exceeding riches of his grace in kindness toward us." Well, conjecturing on a matter so great, I believe that, just as the year's consummation is its last month after which arises another month's beginning, so probably the present age is a consummation of numerous ages completing as it were a year of ages, and after it certain coming ages will arise whose beginning is the coming age. In those coming ages God shall show forth the riches of his grace in kindness, when the greatest sinner, who for having spoken ill against the Holy Spirit is held fast by his sin throughout the present age and the coming one from beginning to end, shall after that, I know not how, receive a dispensation.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: The way which seems right to us for understanding the Scriptures and the investigation of their meaning, we consider to be the following: we are instructed by Scripture itself regarding the ideas that we ought to form of it. In the Proverbs of Solomon we find just such instruction for the examination of holy Scripture. "For your part," he says, "describe these things to yourself in a threefold manner in counsel and knowledge, that you may answer words of truth to those who question you." Each one, then, ought to describe in his own mind, in a threefold manner, the understanding of the divine letters, that is, so that the simple may be edified, so to speak, by the very body of Scripture; for that is what we call the common and historical meaning. But if some have begun to make considerable progress and are able to see something more than that, they may be edified by the very soul of Scripture. And those who are perfect and resemble those of whom the apostle says, "We speak wisdom among them that are perfect, but not the wisdom of this world, nor of the rulers of this world, who are doomed to pass away. But we speak the wisdom of God, hidden in a mystery, which God has decreed before the ages for our glorification." Such people may be edified by the spiritual law which has a shadow of the good things to come, edified as if by the Spirit. For just as man is said to consist of body, and soul and spirit, so also does sacred Scripture, which has been granted by God's gracious dispensation for the salvation of man.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote:
That the first "sense," which we have called the literal one, is profitable in that it is capable of imparting edification is witnessed by the multitude of those believers who accept the faith genuinely and simply. But of that interpretation which is referred back to the "soul," there is an illustration in Paul's first epistle to the Corinthians. He says, "You shall not muzzle the mouth of the ox that treads out the grain." Then he adds, "Is it for oxen that God is concerned? Does he not speak entirely for our sake? It was for our sake, no doubt, that this was written: that the plowman should plough in hope, and the thresher thresh in hope of a share in the crop." And there are numerous interpretations adapted to the multitude which are in circulation, and which edify those who are unable to understand the higher meanings, which have something of the same character. But the interpretation is "spiritual" when one is able to show of what heavenly things the Jews "according to the flesh" served as a copy and a shadow, and of what future blessings the law has a shadow. And, speaking generally, we must investigate, according to the apostolic promise, "the wisdom in a mystery, even the hidden wisdom which God ordained before the world for the glory" of the righteous, which "none of the rulers of this world knew." And the same apostle says somewhere, after mentioning certain events from Exodus and Numbers, "that these things happened to them as a warning, but that they were written down for our instruction, upon whom the end of the ages has come." He also gives hints to show what things these were figures of, when he says, "For they drank of the spiritual Rock that followed them, and that Rock was Christ."11And in another epistle, when outlining the various matters relating to the tabernacle, he used the words: "You shall make everything according to the pattern which was shown you on the mountain." Further, in the epistle to the Galatians, as if reproaching those who think that they are reading the law and yet do not understand it, judging that those do not understand it who do not believe that allegories are contained under what is written, he says: "Tell me, you that desire to be under the law, do you not hear the law? For it is written, Abraham had two sons, one by a slave and one by a free woman. But the son of the slave was born according to the flesh, the son of the free woman through promise. Now this is an allegory: for these women are the two covenants," and so on. Now we must carefully mark each word spoken by him. He says: "You who desire to be under the law" (not "You that are under the law"), "do you not hear the law?"—"hearing" being understood to mean "understanding" and "knowing."
And in the epistle to the Colossians, briefly epitomizing the meaning of the entire system of the law, he says, "Therefore let no man judge you in questions of food and drink, or with regard to a festival or a new moon or a sabbath. These are only a shadow of things to come." Further, in the epistle to the Hebrews, when discoursing about those who belong to the circumcision, he writes, "They serve a copy and shadow of heavenly things." Now it is probable, from these illustrations, that those who have once admitted that the apostle is divinely inspired will entertain no doubt with respect to the five books of Moses; but they wish to know if the rest of the history also "happened figuratively." We must note, then, the expression in the epistle to the Romans, "I have left to myself seven thousand men, who have not bowed the knee to Baal," quoted from the third book of Kings. Paul has understood this to stand for those who are Israelites according to election, for not only are the Gentiles benefited by the coming of Christ, but also some who belong to the divine race.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote:
But if in every detail of this outer covering, that is, the actual history, the sequence of the law had been preserved and its order maintained, we should have understood the Scriptures in an unbroken course and should certainly not have believed that there was anything else buried within them beyond what was indicated at a first glance. Consequently the divine wisdom has arranged for certain stumbling blocks and interruptions of the historical sense to be found therein, by inserting in the midst a number of impossibilities and incongruities. [This was done] in order that the very interruption of the narrative might as it were present a barrier to the reader and lead him to refuse to proceed along the pathway of the ordinary meaning. And so, by shutting us out and debarring us from that, [the writers] might recall us to the beginning of another way, and might thereby bring us, through the entrance of a narrow footpath, to a higher and loftier road and lay open the immense breadth of the divine wisdom.… The aim of the Holy Spirit was chiefly to preserve the connection of the spiritual, meaning, both in the things that are yet to be done and in those which have already been accomplished. [Thus] whenever he found that things which had been done in history could be harmonized with the spiritual meaning, he composed in a single narrative a texture comprising both kinds of meaning, always, however, concealing the secret sense more deeply. But wherever the record of deeds that had been done could not be made to correspond with the sequence of the spiritual truths, he inserted occasionally some deeds of a less probable character or which could not have happened at all, and occasionally some that might have happened but in fact did not. Sometimes he does this by a few words, which in their bodily sense do not appear capable of containing truth and at other times by inserting a large number.This is found to happen particularly in the law, where there are many things that as literal precepts are clearly useful, but also a considerable number in which no principle of utility whatever is disclosed, while sometimes even impossibilities are detected. All this, as we have said, the Holy Spirit supervised, in order that in cases where that which appeared at the first glance could neither be true nor useful we should be led on to search for a truth deeper down and needing more careful examination. And [we] should try to discover in the Scriptures which we believe to be inspired by God a meaning worthy of God.
And not only did the Holy Spirit supervise the writings which were previous to the coming of Christ, but because he is one and the same Spirit and proceeds from the one God, he has acted similarly in regard to the Gospels and the writings of the apostles. For even the narratives that he inspired through them were not woven together without the spell of that wisdom of his, the nature of which we explained above. And so it happens that even in them the Spirit has mingled not a few things by which the historical order of the narrative is interrupted and broken, with the object of turning and calling the attention of the reader, by the impossibility of the literal sense, to an examination of the inner meaning.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: And there is a certain advancement to come from the shadow of the law to the shadow of Christ; so that, because Christ is life, and truth, and the way, we may be made first in the shadow of the way, and in the shadow of life, and in the shadow of truth, that we may comprehend in part, and in a mirror and in an enigma, so that after these things, if we walk along this way, which is Christ, we may be able to arrive at this, that we may comprehend face to face those things which before we had seen as though in a shadow and in an enigma.
source_title: COMMENTARY ON THE SONG OF SONGS, BOOK 3

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: There is, then, the law, and all the things that are in the law, according to the Apostle's judgment, "imposed until the time of correction"; and just as those whose craft it is to make figures out of bronze and to cast statues, before they produce the true work of bronze or of silver or of gold, first form a model of clay after the likeness of the image to come — which model is indeed necessary, but only until the principal work is completed; and when that work has been finished for the sake of which the model of clay had been formed, its use is no longer sought — something of this sort understand also in those things which were either written or done "in a type" and figure of things to come in the law and the prophets. For the very craftsman and author of all things came, and transferred "the law, which had the shadow of the good things to come," to "the very image of the realities."

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: We must also know that just as there is a "law" which contains a "shadow of the good things to come," which have been revealed by the law proclaimed in accordance with truth, so also the gospel, which is thought to be understood by all who read it, teaches a shadow of the mysteries of Christ.And that which John calls an eternal gospel, which would properly be called a spiritual gospel, clearly presents both the mysteries presented by Christ's words and the things of which his acts were symbols, to those who consider "all things face to face" concerning the son of God himself.
source_title: COMMENTARY ON THE GOSPEL OF JOHN 1.39-40

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote:
Paul distinguishes three levels in the law: the shadow, the image and the truth.… The law contains the shadow of future good things but not the very image of the realities, and this clearly shows that the image of the realities is different from what is designated as the shadow of the law. If anyone can describe the ceremonies of the Jewish worship, let him view the temple as not having had the image of realities but only their shadow. Let him see the altar as a mere shadow, and the rams and the calves brought to sacrifice also as a shadow. According to the Scripture, "our days on the earth are like a shadow."If someone wishes to go beyond this shadow, let him come to the image of the realities, and let him behold the coming of Christ made flesh. Let him contemplate him in his role as high priest, offering victims to the Father henceforth and in the future; let him understand that all this is an image of spiritual realities and that heavenly functions are denoted by corporeal functions. We employ the term image to refer to that which is intelligible at present and which human nature can observe.
If you can penetrate the heavens with your understanding and your mind and follow Jesus, who has penetrated the heavens and who stands as our intercessor before the face of God, you will find there those good things whose shadow the law contained and whose image Christ revealed through his incarnation. Those good things … have been prepared for the blessed, which neither eye has seen nor ear heard, and which no person has ever even imagined or thought of.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: In which place I recall that word which the blessed Apostle Paul, writing to the Hebrews, says: "anyone making void the law of Moses dies without any mercy under two or three witnesses; of how much greater punishments will he be thought worthy, who shall have trodden underfoot the Son of God and reckoned the blood of the testament polluted, in which he was sanctified, and done contumely to the Spirit of grace?". But for what cause I have made mention of this scripture, listen. According to the law the adulterer or "adulteress by death used to die", nor could they say: we seek repentance and we implore pardon. There was no place for tears, nor was any faculty of amendment conceded, but it was necessary in every way that he be punished who had incurred the law. And this was observed also in each and every crime to which the penalty of death was appended. Among Christians, however, if adultery has been committed, it is not commanded that the "adulterer or adulteress" be punished with bodily destruction, nor is power given to the bishop of the Church to condemn the adulterer to present death, as then according to the law was done by the elders of the people. What then? Shall we say that the law of Moses is cruel which commands the "adulterer or adulteress" to be punished, and that the gospel of Christ, through indulgence, dissolves its hearers into what is worse? It is not so. For this reason we set forth above the word of Paul saying: "by how much more is he worthy of worse punishments who shall have trodden underfoot the Son of God" and so forth. Hear therefore how neither then was the law cruel, nor now does the gospel seem dissolute on account of the largess of pardon, but in both the kindness of God is maintained by a different dispensation.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: But if you sin again, again the old reproaches are rolled back upon you, all the more so as it is a much greater crime "to trample the Son of God underfoot and to count the blood of the covenant a polluted thing" than to neglect the law of Moses.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: The saints who preceded Jesus' bodily sojourn, who had a somewhat greater mental grasp than the majority of believers, perceived the mysteries of divinity because the word of God was teaching them even before he became flesh, for he was always working, being an imitator of his Father of whom he says, "My Father is working still."He says, perhaps to the Sadducees who do not believe in the doctrine of the resurrection, "Have you not read in the book of Moses, in the passage about the bush, how God said to him, 'I am the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob'? He is not God of the dead, but of the living." If, therefore, God "is not ashamed to be called the God" of these people, and they are numbered among the living by Christ, and all the believers are sons of Abraham, since all the nations are blessed in the faithful Abraham whom God appointed father of the nations, are we hesitant to accept that the living have known the lessons of the living, since they were instructed by Christ, who has existed before the morning star, before he became flesh?
source_title: COMMENTARY ON THE GOSPEL OF JOHN 6.17-18

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Lend your ears here, you who have drawn near to God, you who believe yourselves to be faithful, and consider more diligently how the faith of the faithful is proved by these things that have been read to us. "And it came to pass," it says, "after these words, God tempted Abraham and said to him: Abraham, Abraham. And he said: here I am." Observe each and every thing that is written. For in each single thing, if someone knows how to dig deep, he will find a treasure, and perhaps even where it is not expected the precious jewels of the mysteries lie hidden. This man was formerly called Abram, and nowhere do we read that God called him by this name or said to him: Abram, Abram. For he could not be called by God by a name that was to be abolished, but he calls him by this name that He Himself had bestowed, and He does not only call him by this name, but even doubles it. And when the other had answered, "here I am," He says to him: "take your most beloved son, whom you love, Isaac, and offer him to me. Go," He says, "into the high land, and there offer him as a burnt offering upon one of the mountains, which I will show you." Why God bestowed this name upon him and called him Abraham, He Himself has interpreted: "because," He says, "I have set you as a father of many nations." God gave him this promise when he had a son, Ishmael, but He promised him that in the son who would be born of Sarah this promise would be fulfilled. He had therefore kindled Abraham's own spirit into love of that son, not only for the sake of posterity, but also by the hope of the promises. But this son, in whom these great and marvelous promises were placed for him—this son, I say, in whom his name was called Abraham—he is commanded to offer as a "burnt offering" to the Lord upon one of the mountains. What do you say to this, O Abraham? What and what sort of thoughts are stirred in your heart? A voice has been uttered by God that would shake and prove your faith. What do you say to this? What do you think? What do you reconsider? Do you suppose you turn over in your heart the thought that, if in Isaac the promise was given to me, but I offer this one as a burnt offering, it remains that that promise is not to be hoped for? Or rather do you think these things and say that it is impossible for Him who promised to lie; whatever it may be, the promise will stand firm? But since I "am the least," I am not able to search out the thoughts of so great a patriarch, nor can I know what thoughts the voice of God, which had gone forth to tempt him, stirred in him, what feeling it brought when he was ordered to slay his only son. But since "the spirit of the prophets is subject to the prophets," Paul the Apostle, who through the spirit had learned, I believe, what mind, what counsel Abraham had carried out, indicated it, saying: "by faith Abraham did not hesitate, when he offered his only son, in whom he had received the promises, considering that God is able to raise him even from the dead." The Apostle therefore has disclosed to us the thoughts of the faithful man, that faith in the resurrection had already then begun to be held in Isaac. Abraham therefore hoped that Isaac would rise again and believed that would come to pass which had not yet been done. How then are they "sons of Abraham" who do not believe as accomplished in Christ what he believed as future in Isaac? Nay rather, that I may speak more openly, Abraham knew that he was prefiguring the image of the future truth; he knew that Christ would be born of his seed, who was both to be offered as the truer victim of the whole world and to rise again from the dead.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: This command too is given to her who was once a "harlot": "All," she says, "who shall be found in your house shall be saved. But those who go out of the house — we are free from this oath of yours." If anyone, therefore, wishes to be saved, let him come into this house of her who was once a "harlot." Even if someone from that people wishes to be saved, let him come to this house, that he may be able to obtain salvation. Let him come to this house, in which the blood of Christ is the sign of redemption. For among those who said, "his blood be upon us and upon our children," the blood of Christ is unto condemnation. For Jesus "was set for the fall and for the rising again of many," and therefore, to those who contradict his "sign," "his blood" is made unto punishment, but to those who believe, unto salvation. Let no one, therefore, persuade himself, let no one deceive himself: outside this house, that is, outside the Church, no one is saved; if anyone goes outside, he becomes guilty of his own death. This is the sign of the blood, because here too is the purification which is established through the blood.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Our "Jesus sends" spies to the "king of Jericho," and they are received into lodging by a "harlot." But that harlot, who received the spies sent by Jesus, received them for this reason, that she might no longer be a "harlot." But also the soul of each one of us was a harlot, so long as it lived in the desires and lusts of the flesh. But it received the spies of Jesus, "the angels whom he sent before his face, that they might prepare his way." Yet if each soul received them out of faith, it places them not in lowly places nor in lower ones, but in the higher and lofty ones, because we have received Jesus the Lord not as lowly and earthly, but as one proceeding from the Father and coming from the heavens.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Whatever they feared might bring blame upon the elders, rulers and judges they kept from the knowledge of the people. But some of these things have been preserved in the apocryphal books. For an example we shall give the story about Isaiah, witnessed by the epistle to the Hebrews but not written in any of the canonical books of the Old Testament.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: But let us not omit even that, that it is said not only of Aaron, that "he drink not wine", but also of his sons, when they enter to the holy places. For they have not yet received their gladness—not even the Apostles—but they too wait, that I also may become a partaker of their gladness. For the saints, on departing hence, do not straightway obtain the entire rewards of their merits; but they wait even for us, though we tarry, though we are slothful. For their gladness is not perfect, so long as they grieve over our errors and mourn our sins. Perhaps you may not believe me when I say this; for who am I, that I should dare to affirm the sentence of so great a doctrine? But I bring forward a witness of these things, of whom you cannot doubt: for the "teacher of the Gentiles in faith and truth" is Paul the Apostle. He, then, writing to the Hebrews, when he had enumerated all the holy fathers who were justified through faith, adds after all these also this: "but all these", he says, "having a testimony through faith, did not yet attain the promise, God providing something better for us, that they should not without us attain perfection". You see, therefore, that Abraham still waits, that he may attain the things which are perfect. Isaac too waits, and Jacob, and all the prophets wait for us, that with us they may receive perfect blessedness. On account of this, therefore, that mystery too is kept for the last day of the deferred judgment. For there is "one body" which is awaited to be justified; there is "one body" which is said to rise again in the judgment.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: For the inferior come more quickly into the promise, while the more perfect receive the promises more slowly; and this I shall show from Scripture. Those who received their inheritance under Moses received the promise first, while those who receive their inheritance under Joshua received it later; but also concerning all the righteous it is said, "These all, having obtained witness through faith, did not receive the promise, God having foreseen some better thing concerning us, that they should not be made perfect without us". Is it for this reason that he says without us you have come to reign? For when you, the disciples and hearers, reign, then it is necessary that we too attain to the perfect kingdom of God and of the Lord Jesus.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: This "jealous God", then—if he requires and desires your soul to cleave to him, if he keeps you from sin, if he rebukes, if he chastises, if he is indignant, if he is angry and, as it were, uses a certain jealousy toward you—recognize that there is for you hope of salvation. But if, chastised, you do not come to your senses, if, rebuked, you are not amended, if, scourged, you despise it, know that, if you have so far advanced in sinning, his jealousy will depart from you, and that will be said to you which through the prophet Ezekiel is said to Jerusalem: "therefore my jealousy shall depart from you, and I will be angry over you no more". See the mercy and the loving-kindness of the good God. When he wishes to have mercy, he says that he is indignant and angry, as through Jeremiah he says: "with grief and with scourge you shall be chastised, Jerusalem, lest my soul depart from you". If you understand these things, it is the voice of a God who has mercy, where he is angry, where he is jealous, where he applies griefs and scourges. "For he scourges every son whom he receives".

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: "I will punish with the rod" your saints; "I will visit with a whip their sins." Why? So that "I may not take my mercy from them." For when he leaves someone, he no longer punishes or whips them, since he does not whip everyone, but "every son the Lord receives."

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: We ought, then, to say something also about correction, concerning which the Apostle teaches us generally, saying: "Every correction indeed for the present seems not to be of joy, but of sorrow; but afterward it will yield the most peaceable fruit of righteousness to those who have been exercised by it." And observe even children, how, when they are corrected with blows by their tutors, or are roused by their teachers, they take it grievously indeed, and judge that pain to be the greatest evil which is inflicted upon them for the sake of instruction; and although they are not ignorant that their advancement lies in instructions and corrections of this kind, nevertheless they bear it grievously and impatiently. But if the instruction of children is of this kind, what ought we to think about ourselves who are old, what sort of instruction or correction do we reckon to be hanging over us — one that is inflicted neither by stewards nor by tutors? For Scripture indeed knows the tutor and the steward and the guardian of a little child: what, I say, ought we to suppose or feel, when our instruction and correction has been carried out by the Father of the household himself?

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Nevertheless, with Jesus reciting the law to you and revealing to your hearts the spiritual understanding: neither do you, proselytes, that is, catechumens, remain catechumens any longer, but hasten to receive the grace of God, that you too may be numbered in the assembly of the children of Israel; and you, "children," "do not become boys in your understanding, but in malice be little ones, yet in your understanding be perfect," as the Apostle too says to the Hebrews: "leaving the word of the beginning of Christ, let us be borne on to perfection"; but you also, who under the name of "women" are weak and slack and languid, be admonished, so that you may "raise up the slackened hands and the loosened knees," that is, so that you may rouse your negligent and slothful minds and take up a manly constancy in fulfilling the precepts of the law and the Gospel, and may quickly press on to the perfection of strong men.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: In sacred language God is called a fire, as when Scripture says, "Our God is a consuming fire." Concerning the substance of the angels, it also speaks as follows: "Who makes his angels spirits and his ministers a burning fire." And in another place, "The angel of the Lord appeared in a flame of fire in the bush." In addition, we have received a command to be "fervent in spirit" by which expression undoubtedly the word of God is shown to be hot and fiery. The prophet Jeremiah also hears from him who gave him oracles, "Behold, I am making my words in your mouth a fire." As God, then, is a "fire" and the angels are "flames of fire" and all the saints are "fervent in spirit," so, on the contrary, those who have fallen away from the love of God are undoubtedly said to have cooled in their affection for God and to have become cold.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Many have produced lengthy discussions of God and God's essence. Some have even said that God has a bodily nature that is composed of fine particles and is like ether. Others have said that God is incorporeal and is of a different essence that transcends bodies in dignity and power. For this reason it is worthwhile for us to see if we have resources from the divine Scriptures to say something about God's essence. In John 4:24 it is stated as if God's essence were spirit, for it says, "God is spirit." But in the law, it is instead as if God's essence were fire, for it is written, "Our God is a consuming fire." In John, however, it is stated as if God were light, for John says, "God is light, and in him is no darkness at all." If, then, we should listen to these words literally, making no inquiry beyond the letter, we would have to say that God is a body.… But because we do not see the consequences if we attribute a body to God when we say, even on the basis of Scripture, that God is some such body as spirit, or consuming fire, or light, unless we accept the conclusions that necessarily follow these assertions, we will disgrace ourselves as foolish and contradicting the obvious. For every fire is subject to extinction because it needs fuel; and every spirit, even if we take the spirit to be simple, because it is a body, admits of change to what is coarser in its own nature. In these matters, then, we must either accept so many absurd and blasphemous things about God in preserving the literal meanings, or, as we also do in many other cases, examine and inquire what can be meant when it is said that God is spirit or fire or light. First we must say that just as when we find it written that God has eyes, eyelids, ears, hands, arms, feet, and even wings, we change what is written into an allegory, despising those who bestow on God a form resembling humans; and we do this with good reason. So also must we act consistently with our practice in the case of the names mentioned above.
